passage:
School counsellor's note, stream selection week, Class 10
Zainab came in today with the form half filled: science, like her whole friend group. When I asked what subjects she enjoys, she named history and economics without hesitating, then quickly added, "But everyone's taking science. If I don't, I'll be the only one in a different class." She said the group chat is full of science-coaching plans and she feels sick imagining eating lunch alone. Her friend Samir, she said, told her humanities was "for people who can't do maths." She scored higher in maths than he did. We talked about the difference between choosing a subject and choosing a lunch table. She asked for a day to think and to talk to her parents. I will meet her again on Thursday.

qa.q: Which subjects does Zainab enjoy?
qa.a: History and economics.

qa.q: Why is Zainab about to choose science?
qa.a: She feels anxious about standing out and eating lunch alone, so following the friend group feels safer than choosing what she enjoys.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Zainab separate, and why does it help?
qa.a: Choosing a subject from choosing a lunch table, so the decision is about her interests and not only the group.

qa.q: How might Samir's comment have affected Zainab?
qa.a: It probably made her feel more pressured and a bit small, even though she scored higher in maths than he did.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage girl about to choose a stream because her whole group has, anxious about being the only one in a different class.

passage:
Saturday night
The whole class is doing the umbrella dance trend. Every single person has posted one. Even Sachin, who hates dancing, posted his yesterday with his little brother. My feed is just umbrellas.
I don't want to do it. I feel stupid dancing and I hate how I look in videos. But today at lunch Meghna said, "Usha's the only one left," and everyone laughed, and I laughed too, and my stomach felt like it was folding.
So tonight I filmed it eleven times in the bathroom. I posted the least bad one. Twelve likes so far. I feel relieved and also kind of gross, like I did it for them, not for me.
Maybe I'll ask Sachin tomorrow if he actually wanted to.
Usha

qa.q: How many times did Usha film the video?
qa.a: Eleven times, in the bathroom.

qa.q: How does Usha feel after posting the video?
qa.a: Usha feels relieved and also kind of gross, sensing it was done to fit in rather than out of wanting to.

qa.q: What might help Usha the next time a trend sweeps the class?
qa.a: Asking whether it is wanted or only done to avoid standing out, and talking honestly with a friend like Sachin who may feel the same.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sachin to post the trend?
qa.a: Sachin hates dancing too, so he may also have felt pushed into it by everyone else posting.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows joining a class trend they dislike because being the only one left feels unbearable.

passage: Ishita, you say you'll join because everyone in the hostel already has? Let your Madhuri maasi tell you about the year I was nineteen, in a hostel in Nagpur. Suddenly every girl on our floor was selling soaps and creams for some company. They paid to join and then got others to join. There were meetings with music and a man in a shiny suit. Forty girls, then sixty. I thought, sixty people can't all be wrong, and I gave my whole scholarship to join. Six months later the office was locked and the man was gone. Sixty of us had been wrong together. Your nana didn't shout. He just asked, "Did you check what they actually sold, or only how many were buying?" I've asked that question about everything since.

qa.q: What did young Madhuri give to join?
qa.a: Her whole scholarship.

qa.q: Why did young Madhuri believe the scheme was safe?
qa.a: She felt reassured and excited because sixty girls had joined, so the crowd felt like proof it was genuine.

qa.q: What question from the story could have changed the choice, and why?
qa.a: "Did you check what they actually sold, or only how many were buying?" It points to real evidence instead of the crowd.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's father have felt when the office was locked?
qa.a: He was probably worried and sad for her, yet chose to ask a gentle question rather than shout.

grounding: An aunt recalls joining a scheme at nineteen because sixty hostel mates had, treating popularity as proof, and losing her scholarship.

passage: Voting in the student union election closed at four, and it was 3:50 when Anirban ran into the hall, out of breath. "Who are you voting for?" asked Rajni, standing in the queue. "Pritam, obviously. Everyone's voting Pritam. His posters are everywhere, and he's got the most followers." "What's he promising?" Anirban opened his mouth. "Something about the canteen? I don't know. But five hundred people can't be wrong." "Five hundred people might all have the same reason as you," Rajni said. The queue moved. Anirban took out his phone and, with seven minutes left, opened the two manifestos for the first time. Pritam's was one page of slogans. The other candidate's had a plan for the short library hours he complained about every week. At 3:58 he stood in the booth, pen hovering.

qa.q: What time did voting close?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why was Anirban sure about voting for Pritam?
qa.a: He felt confident because Pritam's posters and followers were everywhere, so popularity seemed like proof he was the right choice.

qa.q: What did Anirban do in the last minutes, and why was it useful?
qa.a: He opened both manifestos for the first time, which let him judge the actual plans rather than how many people liked Pritam.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the five hundred votes?
qa.a: Rajni thinks they might all share Anirban's reason, following the crowd rather than checking.

grounding: Minutes before voting closes, a student backs the most popular candidate because 'five hundred people can't be wrong'.

passage: In the Koramangala office canteen, everyone was talking about the same thing: a new coin on a trading app that had "gone up four times in a month." Dolma, three months into her first job, listened to five colleagues describe their profits. By evening she had the app open and her savings ready to move. "If everyone's in, it can't be a scam," she told her flatmate Chetan. Chetan looked over. "What does the coin actually do?" Dolma scrolled. "It... has a community?" "And how many people lost money on the last three coins everyone was talking about?" She didn't know. She closed the app, a little annoyed, and called her cousin, who worked as a financial adviser. "Don't decide tonight," the cousin said. "Let's go through it on Sunday."

qa.q: What did colleagues say the coin had done?
qa.a: Gone up four times in a month.

qa.q: Why did Dolma think the coin couldn't be a scam?
qa.a: She felt reassured and excited because so many colleagues were in, so popularity felt like evidence that it was safe.

qa.q: What did Dolma do before moving her savings, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She closed the app and called her cousin, a financial adviser, to go through it on Sunday, instead of following the crowd that night.

qa.q: How does Chetan see the coin?
qa.a: Chetan is doubtful, wanting to know what the coin actually does and what happened with past popular coins.

grounding: A young woman nearly follows colleagues into a popular coin, treating popularity as proof, until a question and a qualified adviser slow her down.

passage:
Monday. The whole team signed up for the office marathon: matching T-shirts, a group chat called RUN SQUAD, a photo for the company page. Arohi's name went on the list before she had even thought. "Obviously you're in," said Chetan.
Wednesday. At the first practice run, Arohi's knees ached and she felt nothing but dread. That night she sat with a notebook and asked herself two questions. Why do I want this? Because everyone else is doing it. What would I choose if nobody ever knew? Swimming, early mornings, alone.
Saturday. Arohi told Chetan she was stepping out of the marathon and would be at the finish line with water and banners instead. He looked surprised, then grinned. "Cheer squad needs a captain." On Sunday morning she swam forty lengths and felt lighter than she had all week.

qa.q: What would Arohi choose if nobody ever knew?
qa.a: Swimming, early mornings, alone.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling at the first practice run?
qa.a: She felt aching knees and nothing but dread, a sign the marathon wasn't really her choice.

qa.q: How did Arohi decide, and why is it a good way?
qa.a: She asked why she wanted it and what she would choose if nobody knew, then stepped out deliberately while staying connected as cheer captain.

qa.q: How did Chetan react to Arohi stepping out?
qa.a: He was surprised, then grinned and made her captain of the cheer squad.

grounding: Over a week, a young woman asks why she joined the office crowd and what she would pick if nobody knew, then leaves it deliberately.

passage: Bhupen, you think going along with the crowd is always weak? Let your Mahima didi tell you what happened when I was twenty-four. Every single person in my nursing batch was applying to the same government hospital. I nearly applied somewhere else just to be different. Then my mother asked me two questions: "Why do you want the other place?" and "If nobody ever knew what you chose, which one would you pick?" I sat on the terrace till midnight. Honest answer: I wanted to be different only so people would notice. And if nobody knew, I'd pick the government hospital, because of its maternity ward. So I joined the crowd, but on purpose this time. Twenty years later, I still run that ward. Sometimes the crowd is right. The point is to know why you're in it.

qa.q: Which ward made Mahima choose the government hospital?
qa.a: The maternity ward.

qa.q: Why did young Mahima nearly apply somewhere else?
qa.a: She felt tempted to stand out, wanting to be different only so people would notice, not because she wanted that place.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mahima's story?
qa.a: Her mother's two questions, which showed she really wanted the government hospital, so she joined the crowd deliberately.

qa.q: What might Mahima's mother have felt when she chose?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and relieved that Mahima chose for her own reasons.

grounding: A senior nurse recalls asking why she wanted a choice and what she would pick if nobody knew, then joining the crowd on purpose.

passage: The tailor needed final orders by nine the next morning, and at 11 p.m. the bridesmaids' group chat was still buzzing: all seven had chosen the same pink lehenga for Gargi's sangeet, and everyone was waiting for Nikita. "Just say yes!!" someone wrote. Nikita's thumb hovered. The lehenga was lovely, but it was pricey and she would never wear it again. She put the phone face down and asked herself: Why do I want this? So I don't look like the odd one out. And if nobody would ever know? I'd wear my mother's old green silk and spend the money on Gargi's gift. At 11:40 she messaged Gargi privately, not the group. Gargi replied in a minute: "Wear the green. You'll glow. I just want you there."

qa.q: What would Nikita wear if nobody knew?
qa.a: Her mother's old green silk.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's thumb hover over the chat?
qa.a: She felt torn and a bit anxious, liking the lehenga but not wanting to buy it only to avoid looking like the odd one out.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that made her choice deliberate?
qa.a: She put the phone down, asked why she wanted it and what she would choose if nobody knew, then messaged Gargi privately.

qa.q: How did Gargi respond to Nikita's message?
qa.a: Gargi was warm and supportive, telling Nikita to wear the green and that she just wanted her there.

grounding: Under a deadline, a young woman asks why she wants to match the group and what she would choose if nobody knew, then decides.

subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]
passage: In the Class 4 science period, Mrs Rao wrote on the board: "Spiders are insects." Kishore's pencil stopped. At home he had a picture book that said, in big letters, that spiders have eight legs and are not insects. He even remembered the page. But Mrs Rao was the teacher, and she had been teaching for twenty years. Maybe the book was old. He copied the sentence into his notebook, ears hot. Beside him, Dilnaz put up her hand. "Ma'am, don't insects have six legs?" The class went quiet. Kishore's stomach tightened; he was sure Dilnaz would be scolded. Mrs Rao looked at the board, then laughed. "You're right. I meant to write arachnids. Well spotted." Kishore looked down at the wrong sentence in his own neat handwriting.

qa.q: What did Kishore's picture book say about spiders?
qa.a: That spiders have eight legs and are not insects.

qa.q: Why did Kishore copy the wrong sentence anyway?
qa.a: He felt afraid to question Mrs Rao, respecting her twenty years so much that he doubted his own book.

qa.q: How could Kishore question a teacher respectfully next time?
qa.a: Ask a polite question, as Dilnaz did, such as "Don't insects have six legs?", which checks the fact without being rude.

qa.q: How did Mrs Rao react to Dilnaz's question?
qa.a: Mrs Rao laughed, admitted the mistake and praised Dilnaz for spotting it.

grounding: A boy copies a teacher's wrong statement though his own book says otherwise, too afraid to question her.

passage:
Monday. Rajni aunty, the retired headmistress next door, told Vandana on the stairs that the Great Wall of China could be seen from the moon. "Every astronaut says so." Vandana nodded. Rajni aunty knew everything.
Wednesday. In the school library, Vandana found a space book with a whole box about it: "Myth! The wall is too narrow to see from the moon." She read it three times. Her chest felt tight. Either the book was wrong, or Rajni aunty was. And you did not tell Rajni aunty she was wrong.
Saturday. Vandana carried the book up the stairs, then down again, then up. Finally she knocked. "Aunty, I found something. Can I show you?" Rajni aunty read the box, put on her glasses and read it again. "Well," she said slowly. "I've been telling people that for forty years." Then she smiled. "Thank you, beta."

qa.q: What did the library book say about the Great Wall?
qa.a: Myth! The wall is too narrow to see from the moon.

qa.q: Why did Vandana's chest feel tight in the library?
qa.a: She felt afraid, because the book said Rajni aunty was wrong, and you did not tell Rajni aunty she was wrong.

qa.q: How did Vandana finally raise it, and why did it work?
qa.a: She knocked and asked to show aunty something, letting the book speak politely, so respect and truth could go together.

qa.q: How did Rajni aunty react?
qa.a: She was surprised after forty years of repeating it, but smiled and thanked Vandana.

grounding: Over a week, a girl who believes an elder is always right finds a book that says otherwise and is afraid to question her.

passage: Ishita, you're afraid to tell your tuition sir his answer is wrong? Let your Nilesh dadu tell you about the train to Ranchi. I was ten, and my Bade Chacha was taking me to my grandmother's. He was the eldest in the family; nobody argued with him. At the station he said, "The train is at six." I had read the timetable board myself on the way in: 5:30. I knew it. But I thought, who am I to correct Bade Chacha? So I sat quietly on the bench eating peanuts. At 5:35 the train pulled out right in front of us. Bade Chacha stood up, astonished. I burst into tears and said, "I saw 5:30." He wasn't angry. He said, "Next time, tell me. Being right is not rudeness." We waited nine hours for the next one.

qa.q: What time did the timetable board say?
Why did young Nilesh keep quiet about the timetable?
qa.a: He felt afraid to correct Bade Chacha, the eldest in the family, so respect and fear kept him silent even though he knew.

qa.q: What moment in the story changed how Nilesh saw speaking up?
qa.a: When Bade Chacha said, "Next time, tell me. Being right is not rudeness," after they missed the train.

qa.q: How did Bade Chacha seem to feel when the train pulled out?
qa.a: He was astonished but not angry, and chose to teach Nilesh that speaking up is not rude.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, at ten, fear of contradicting an elder kept him silent about the right train time.

passage: At the athletics club in Stockholm, Coach Anders was known for two things: winning medals and never being questioned. On the hottest day of the summer he told the group, "No water breaks today. Thirsty runners get tough." Nkechi, fifteen, felt her mouth go dry just hearing it. In biology last month they had learned that the body needs water when it sweats. But Anders had coached national runners. Who was she to argue? After the third lap her head started to pound. She stopped by the fence, face hot with embarrassment, and said, "Coach, I'm sorry, but my biology teacher said we need water in heat. Can I drink?" A few runners stared. Anders frowned, then waved a hand. "Fine. Everyone, two minutes." Nkechi drank, cheeks still burning, and her head began to clear.

qa.q: What did Coach Anders say about water?
qa.a: No water breaks today; thirsty runners get tough.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi's cheeks burn when she spoke up?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and nervous questioning a famous coach, even though she trusted what she had learned in biology.

qa.q: What made Nkechi's question respectful and effective?
qa.a: She apologised, gave her reason from biology and asked a simple question, so it didn't sound like an attack.

qa.q: How might the other runners feel after the water break?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and grateful, since they got water too because Nkechi spoke up.

grounding: A teenage girl weighs a famous coach's confident claim against what she learned in biology, and awkwardly questions it.

passage: The school auditorium was packed for the famous guest speaker, a young man with two million followers and a gold watch. "Toppers sleep four hours," he announced. "Sleep is for losers. I never slept in Class 12." Everyone cheered. Ojas wrote it down in capitals. That night he stayed up till 3 a.m. with physics, and the next day he fell asleep in the lab and spilled a beaker. Aditi ma'am, the biology teacher, sat with him at lunch. "Where did the four-hour idea come from?" "The speaker. He's really successful." "At what?" Ojas thought. "At... videos?" "Did he show any evidence about sleep?" Ojas felt his face go red. He had believed a gold watch. "No, ma'am." "Let's look at what the research says together," she said.

qa.q: What happened to Ojas in the lab the next day?
qa.a: He fell asleep and spilled a beaker.

qa.q: Why did Ojas's face go red at lunch?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising he had believed the speaker because of fame and a gold watch, with no evidence about sleep.

qa.q: What questions did Aditi ma'am ask, and why are they useful?
qa.a: Successful at what, and did he show evidence; they help Ojas separate someone's fame from whether a claim is true.

qa.q: How might Aditi ma'am feel about the speaker's message?
qa.a: She was probably concerned, since students like Ojas were copying an unhealthy idea.

grounding: A teenage boy believes a famous speaker's confident claim about sleep, then awkwardly learns that fame is not evidence.

passage:
Dear Kalyani didi,
I need advice. Papa has started following a man in the family chat group who calls himself a "retired senior bank manager" and posts share tips every morning. Papa says, "He was a bank manager, he knows." Yesterday Papa said he might put some of the savings into the man's "guaranteed" pick.
I looked the man up. I couldn't find any bank he worked at. Also, our economics teacher said nobody honest promises guaranteed returns. But how do I tell Papa that? He's my father. He's always right about things like this. When I tried at dinner it came out wrong, and he said, "You're sixteen, what do you know?"
Can you call him? Or tell me how to say it without it sounding rude?
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did the economics teacher say?
qa.a: That nobody honest promises guaranteed returns.

qa.q: Why does Ujjwal find it hard to tell Papa?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels awkward and unsure, respecting Papa as always right, and the first try at dinner came out wrong.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal doing that is wise?
qa.a: Checking the man's claims and asking Kalyani didi, a trusted adult, to call Papa or help find respectful words.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if Kalyani calls him?
qa.a: Papa might feel defensive at first, but may listen more easily to an adult he respects.

grounding: A teenager weighs a parent's trust in a self-styled expert against evidence and awkwardly seeks a trusted adult's help.

passage: On the fourth floor of the half-built tower in Pune, the senior supervisor, Kunal sir, waved at Irfan. "Harness takes too long. Just go up the scaffold and fix that pipe. Five minutes." Irfan, three weeks into his traineeship, looked at the harness hanging on the rail. The safety rule on the notice board downstairs said always. But Kunal sir had fifteen years on sites, and everyone called him Guru. Saying no felt like slapping him. Irfan climbed without it. Halfway up, a plank shifted under his foot. He grabbed a pipe and hung there, heart hammering, until two workers pulled him in. The safety officer, who had seen it from below, came up at once, stopped work on that floor and took Irfan and Kunal sir into the site office. "Nobody climbs without a harness. Nobody tells anyone to," she said.

qa.q: What did Kunal sir tell Irfan to skip?
qa.a: The harness.

qa.q: Why did Irfan climb without the harness?
qa.a: He admired Kunal sir's fifteen years and felt that refusing would be disrespectful, like slapping him, so fear of offending outweighed the rule.

qa.q: What could Irfan have said to object politely?
qa.a: Something like "Sir, I'll be quick, but the rule says always; can I put it on first?", which respects both the senior and the safety rule.

qa.q: How did the safety officer respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She stopped the work at once and spoke to both of them, making clear that nobody climbs without a harness or tells others to.

grounding: A young trainee follows a respected senior's unsafe instruction because refusing feels disrespectful, and a safety officer steps in.

passage:
"Uma, just change the date on this bill to March. The client wants it in last year's accounts."
"Change the date, sir?"
"It's a small thing. Everyone does it."
"But the purchase was in April. The stamp says April."
Divyansh sir sighed. "You're new. Trust me. This is how the real world works."
Uma looked at the bill. Her hand moved towards the pen. He was the senior; she was the trainee. He had been here eight years. Saying no felt like calling him a cheat.
"Sir," she said, her voice small, "can I check with the partner first? Just so I learn the rule properly?"
He frowned. "You're making it a big deal."
"I'm sorry, sir. I just don't want either of us in trouble."
He looked at her for a long moment, then took the bill back. "Leave it. I'll ask the client for an April entry."

qa.q: What month did the stamp on the bill say?
qa.a: April.

qa.q: Why did Uma's hand move toward the pen?
qa.a: She felt pressured and afraid of seeming disrespectful to a senior with eight years there, as if saying no would call him a cheat.

qa.q: What made Uma's objection work?
qa.a: She asked to check with the partner to learn the rule and said she didn't want either of them in trouble, which was polite but firm.

qa.q: How might Divyansh sir feel after taking the bill back?
qa.a: He may feel irritated but also caught out, realising the trainee won't quietly change dates.

grounding: A young trainee nearly follows a senior's instruction to backdate a bill because refusing feels disrespectful, then finds a polite way to object.

passage: In my first month as a trainee at the textile dyeing unit, the senior chemist, Preeti ma'am, handed me two buckets of used dye. "Pour them in the drain behind the shed. Quickly, before the inspector comes on Monday." I knew that drain ran into the canal where kids swam. I knew we had a treatment tank for exactly this. But Preeti ma'am had trained half the unit, and everyone stood up when she walked in. I couldn't find a single polite way to say no, so I said nothing. I poured them. For a week I couldn't look at the canal. Then I told the plant manager everything, my part included. The unit was fined, and so was she. People were cold to me for months. Vishal, the one who told. I'd still rather be him than the one who kept pouring.

qa.q: Where did the drain behind the shed run?
qa.a: Into the canal where kids swam.

qa.q: Why did Vishal pour the dye without saying anything?
qa.a: He admired and feared Preeti ma'am's standing and couldn't find a polite way to say no, so objecting felt impossible.

qa.q: What could Vishal have said at the time?
qa.a: A polite question like "Ma'am, shouldn't this go in the treatment tank? Can I take it there?", respecting her while refusing the harmful act.

qa.q: How might the children who swim in the canal be affected?
qa.a: They could be harmed by the dye water, which is why Vishal's later report mattered.

grounding: A young trainee recalls following a respected senior's harmful instruction because refusing felt impossible, and reporting it later.

passage:
Department head's note, design review, 9 September
In today's review, our chief engineer, Tarun sir, said the new drainage layout "will never flood; I've built twenty like it." Harsha, two years into the job, raised a hand. "Sir, I've learned a lot from those twenty. May I ask how the rainfall figure was chosen for this one?" Tarun sir said it was the standard figure. Harsha then showed, politely and without fuss, last year's rainfall records for this district, which were higher than the standard, and asked whether we should check the pipe size against them. The room was quiet. Tarun sir looked at the records for a while and said, "Run it again with these." After the meeting Harsha thanked him for listening. I have asked Harsha to present the revised check on Friday.

qa.q: How many similar layouts had Tarun sir built?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What does Harsha's opening line suggest about Harsha's attitude?
qa.a: Harsha feels real admiration for Tarun sir's experience, while still being confident enough to question the rainfall figure.

qa.q: How did Harsha separate respect from agreement?
qa.a: By honouring Tarun sir's experience, asking how the figure was chosen and offering records politely, rather than attacking the claim.

qa.q: How might Tarun sir have felt looking at the records?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a little uneasy, but respected enough to agree to run it again.

grounding: A department head records a young engineer asking how a senior's claim was reached and offering evidence politely.

passage:
Thursday
Big meeting today. Kalyani ma'am, our head of customer service, said we should shut down chat support because "customers hate typing; they only want phone calls." She's brilliant, and I've learned more from her than from anyone.
But I had the numbers from last quarter: chat got higher satisfaction scores than phone, and most chats came from people under thirty.
My heart was racing. I said, "Ma'am, can I ask how we know customers hate it? I pulled some numbers that surprised me." I showed the chart. She was quiet for a bit, then asked, "Where did you get these?" I told her. She said, "Send them to me. Let's not shut it yet."
After, I told her I'd learned to read these reports from her. She laughed.
Raghav

qa.q: Which support channel got higher satisfaction scores?
qa.a: Chat.

qa.q: How was Raghav feeling before speaking up?
qa.a: Raghav felt nervous, heart racing, out of admiration for Kalyani ma'am, yet confident enough in the numbers to ask.

qa.q: What made Raghav's challenge respectful?
qa.a: Asking how they knew customers hated chat, sharing the chart as a surprise rather than a gotcha, and thanking her afterwards.

qa.q: How did Kalyani ma'am respond?
qa.a: She was quiet, asked where the numbers came from, and agreed not to shut chat yet.

grounding: A young professional asks a respected senior how a claim was reached, offers data politely and keeps respect separate from agreement.

passage: When I became the youngest branch manager in our company, I was proud that meetings went so smoothly. Every idea I suggested, everyone agreed with. Then in March a project I had pushed failed badly, and afterwards Naveen, our most experienced clerk, said quietly, "Joseph sir, some of us saw it coming." I asked why nobody had said so. He looked at the floor. "You're the manager." That hit me hard. My title was doing the talking and switching everyone else off. So I changed how meetings start. Before I say anything, each person writes one worry on a slip, and we read them out without names. And whenever someone brings me bad news, I thank them out loud, in front of the team. Last week Naveen told me our new form was confusing. I said thank you. He smiled.

qa.q: What does each person write before the manager speaks?
qa.a: One worry on a slip.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Naveen said "You're the manager"?
qa.a: Joseph felt shaken and a bit ashamed, realising the title had been silencing people.

qa.q: What two changes did Joseph make, and why do they work?
qa.a: Anonymous worry slips at the start of meetings and thanking people publicly for bad news, which make disagreement feel safe.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel being thanked for pointing out the confusing form?
qa.a: Naveen probably feels respected and more confident to speak, as his smile suggests.

grounding: A young manager recalls realising his title silenced staff, and how he began inviting worries early and thanking bad news.

passage:
Leadership coach's note, session four with Darshan, 3 June
Darshan, six months into leading the product team, told me today that his meetings had become "too quiet." He had noticed that nobody disagreed with him, even about a launch plan he suspected was weak. He said he used to think this meant he was right. Now he thinks his title is muting people. This week he tried two things we had discussed. He asked for concerns before sharing his own view, and he thanked people publicly for bad news. On Thursday, Zainab from testing told the whole meeting that the launch build was failing on older phones. He thanked her in front of everyone and moved the date. He said it felt uncomfortable, and right. We will review how the team responds next month.

qa.q: What problem did Zainab report?
qa.a: The launch build was failing on older phones.

qa.q: How did thanking Zainab feel for Darshan?
qa.a: It felt uncomfortable and right to him, awkward but in line with the kind of leader he wants to be.

qa.q: What two things did Darshan try, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking for concerns before giving his own view, and thanking people publicly for bad news, which makes it safer to disagree.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel after being thanked in the meeting?
qa.a: Zainab probably felt relieved and valued, having risked bringing bad news in front of everyone.

grounding: A coach records a young leader noticing his title mutes his team, inviting concerns early and thanking a colleague for bad news.

passage:
Tuesday, after closing
Third week as head chef, and I finally noticed something. When I ask "Any problems?" at the morning briefing, everyone says, "No, chef." Every day. Then at 9 p.m. things go wrong that clearly someone knew about. Today the fridge had been making a noise for four days, and nobody told me until it died.
Gurpreet said to me afterwards, "Chef, people don't want to be the one who brings you bad news." I didn't know I was that scary. I think it's the title, not me. Or both.
Tomorrow I'm changing the briefing. I'll ask, "What's the one thing most likely to go wrong today?" and go round the whole line, starting with the newest. Whoever brings bad news first gets a thank-you on the board.
Tanvir

qa.q: How long had the fridge been making a noise?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What did Tanvir feel on hearing Gurpreet's explanation?
qa.a: Tanvir felt surprised and a little uneasy, not having realised the title made people too scared to speak.

qa.q: How is Tanvir changing the briefing, and why?
qa.a: Asking what is most likely to go wrong, going round the line starting with the newest, and thanking the first bearer of bad news on the board, so speaking up feels safe.

qa.q: How might the newest cook feel being asked first?
qa.a: The newest cook might feel nervous but also taken seriously, with a real chance to speak before the seniors set the tone.

grounding: A young head chef's diary shows noticing that the title keeps staff silent, and planning to invite bad news early and thank it.

passage:
PE teacher's note, inter-house football, Friday
Kamal (Class 5, Blue House) was very loud today. When Blue's captain pushed Sharmila from Yellow House in the box, Kamal shouted, "That's fine, that's football!" Ten minutes later, when a Yellow player pushed a Blue player in exactly the same way, Kamal ran to the touchline yelling, "Cheating! Red card!" Sharmila heard both and asked him, "So pushing is only cheating when we do it?" Kamal said Blue's push was "an accident." After the match I sat both houses down and replayed the two moments on my phone, one after the other, without saying which house was which. Kamal said the first one was a foul. It was Blue's. He was quiet for a while. We will talk about fair play in Monday's PE lesson.

qa.q: What did Kamal shout when Blue's captain pushed Sharmila?
qa.a: "That's fine, that's football!"

qa.q: Why did Kamal call the Blue push an accident?
qa.a: He felt proud and loyal to Blue House, so his own team's push seemed innocent while the same act by Yellow felt like cheating.

qa.q: Why did replaying both moments without the house names help?
qa.a: It let Kamal judge the pushes on what actually happened, so he could see Blue's was also a foul.

qa.q: How did Sharmila see Kamal's reactions?
qa.a: Sharmila saw the unfairness and challenged him, asking if pushing was only cheating when Yellow did it.

grounding: A PE teacher records a boy excusing his own house's foul while calling the same act cheating by the other house.
